'''''Petrosedum sediforme''''', the '''pale stonecrop''', is a [[perennial]] [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Crassulaceae]]. It is naturally distributed throughout the [[Mediterranean Basin]], from Portugal in the west to Syria in the east. It is similar to other species of ''[[Petrosedum]]'', but grows taller, and may be used in cooking or as an [[ornamental plant]].

==Distribution==
The natural range of ''Petrosedum sediforme'' extends throughout the [[Mediterranean Basin]].<ref name="Eggli"/> It is found in Portugal, Spain, France, Italy, and [[Mediterranean islands]], as well as Turkey, Palestine, Israel, Libya, Syria, Tunisia, Algeria, and Morocco. It typically grows in lowland areas, often near the sea on [[dune]]s or [[coastal cliff]]s, but it can also be found at higher elevations, reaching up to 1000 meters in the [[French Alps]] and 1750 meters in the [[Sierra Nevada (Spain)|Sierra Nevada]].<ref name="Stephenson">{{cite book | last=Stephenson | first=Ray | title=Sedum: Cultivated Stonecrops | publisher=Timber Press | year=1994| isbn=978-1-60469-100-9 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=P5GGPwAACAAJ | access-date=2 February 2025 | page=123-124}}</ref> It prefers open, sunny habitats,<ref name="Smith"/> but [[ecological tolerance|tolerates]] a wide range of climates and environmental conditions.<ref name="Gideon">{{cite journal | last=Smith | first=Gideon F. | title=Notes on the fire ecology of Petrosedum Grulich and Sedum L. (Crassulaceae) in central continental Portugal | journal=Bradleya | volume=36 | issue=36 | date=2018 | issn=0265-086X | doi=10.25223/brad.n36.2018.a8 | pages=61–69| bibcode=2018Bradl..36...61S }}</ref> It is commonly (but not exclusively) found in [[limestone]].<ref name="Ray">{{cite journal | last=Stephenson | first=Ray | title=Portuguese succulents | journal=Cactus and Succulent Journal | volume=79 | issue=6 | date=2007 | issn=0007-9367 | doi=10.2985/0007-9367(2007)79[265:PS]2.0.CO;2 | pages=265–268}}</ref>

Specimens of ''Petrosedum sediforme'' have been found with varying [[chromosome count]]s, including 2n=32/48/60/64/96.<ref name="Eggli"/> Diploid forms (2n=32) are generally confined to lowland environments. Hexaploids (2n=96) predominantly inhabit mountainous areas, whereas tetraploids (2n=64) show no distinct habitat preference. A striking [[cristate]] form, propagated from seed, has been introduced in [[horticulture]].<ref name="Stephenson"/> A naturally occurring [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] between ''[[Petrosedum forsterianum]]'' and ''P. sediforme'' was discovered in Portugal and described in 2015 as ''[[Petrosedum × estrelae]]''.<ref name="Smith">{{cite journal | last1=Smith | first1=Gideon F. |last2=Stephenson | first2=Ray | title=''Petrosedum×estrelae'' Gideon F.Sm. & R.Stephenson (Crassulaceae) [''Petrosedum forsterianum'' (Sm.) Grulich × ''Petrosedum sediforme'' (Jacq.) Grulich]: a new nothospecies from central Portugal | journal=Bradleya | publisher=British Cactus and Succulent Society | volume=33 | issue=33 | date=20 October 2015 | issn=0265-086X | doi=10.25223/brad.n33.2015.a2 | pages=2–8| bibcode=2015Bradl..33....2S }}</ref>

==Description==
''Petrosedum sediforme'' is a branching species with often woody, non-flowering basal shoots. Leaves are overlapping, oblong to elliptic, with pointed tips, somewhat thickened, sometimes flattened and spurred, reaching up to 20 mm in length. They are smooth, dark green, and often [[glaucous]].<ref name="Eggli"/> Because its leaves are remarkably [[succulent]], the species does not go through [[dormancy]] during the summer.<ref name="Ray"/>

When in bloom, ''Petrosedum sediforme'' produces upright flowering stems that range from 25 to 60 cm tall. The flowers grow in clusters at the top of the stem, with each flower attached by a very short stalk or none at all. The small green triangular [[sepal]]s (the outer parts that protect the flower bud) are about 2–3 mm long. The [[petal]]s are oblong, greenish-white to creamy in color, and about 5–8 mm long. The plant usually has 6–8 petals per flower, rarely 5 or 9. The [[stamen]]s (the parts that hold [[pollen]]) have white filaments with a rough texture at the base and yellow [[anther]]s.<ref name="Eggli"/> The flowers are produced in mid-summer.<ref name="Smith"/> They are followed by erect, dark brown fruit. Seeds are oblong, brown, and ribbed.<ref name="Eggli">{{cite book | last=Eggli | first=Urs | title=Illustrated Handbook of Succulent Plants: Crassulaceae | publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg | year=2012 | isbn=978-3-642-55874-0 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nU7mCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA201 | access-date=2 February 2025 | page=316}}</ref>

''Petrosedum sediforme'' is difficult to distinguish from ''[[Petrosedum rupestre|P. rupestre]]'', ''[[Petrosedum ochroleucum|P. ochroleucum]]'', and ''[[Petrosedum montanum|P. montanum]]'' based solely on vegetative traits.<ref name="Stephenson"/> Spanish plants with brownish or olive-green tones are remarkably similar to some Israeli specimens—despite originating from the opposite end of the species’ range. In the Sierra Nevada, even plants growing side by side can exhibit striking differences.<ref name="Stephenson"/>

==Uses==
[[File:Petrosedum sediforme 445472290.jpg|thumb|upright|Glaucous forms are particularly valued in horticulture.]]
''Petrosedum sediforme'' is sometimes cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]] in [[rock garden]]s.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_w_9TBFiSqgC&pg=PA246 |title=Waterwise Plants for Sustainable Gardens: 200 Drought-Tolerant Choices for all Climates |last1=Ogden |first1=Scott |last2=Ogden |first2=Lauren Springer |date=2011-11-03 |publisher=Timber Press |isbn=9781604693362 |pages=130 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Petrosedum sediforme (Jacq.) Grulich |url=https://www.catalogueoflife.org/data/taxon/6V8CK |publisher=[[Catalogue of Life]] |access-date=24 March 2021}}</ref> Forms with broad leaves from Portugal and Spain are particularly valued for their compact growth, and those with glaucous leaves are particularly popular. In contrast, those from higher elevations in France are more resilient, although they lack the same visual appeal. Compared to other ''Petrosedum'' species, ''P. sediforme'' has a more refined appearance, but it also has a tendency to grow tall.<ref name="Stephenson"/> The species is edible; its leaves may be used in cooking as a [[pot-herb]].<ref name="Kunkel">{{cite book | last=Kunkel | first=Günther | title=Plants for Human Consumption: An Annotated Checklist of the Edible Phanerogams and Ferns | publisher=Koeltz Scientific Books | year=1984 | isbn=978-3-87429-216-0 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7L0H0WBBMOkC&pg=PA333 | access-date=31 January 2025 | page=328}}</ref>
